Planning as value updates on simulated experience, and the Dyna-Q architecture

intro.why: Using a model to plan can make learning dramatically more sample-efficient, and combining search with learned networks produced some of RL's landmark results in games. The same ideas underpin world-model agents and test-time search.
prereq: Session M4 (DP, planning with a model)

symbols: parent and child visit counts in MCTS

sections.title: Model-free vs model-based; kinds of models
sections.plain: A model predicts what the environment will do; planning uses it to improve the policy without acting.
sections.body:
A model is anything the agent can use to predict how the environment responds to its actions. Distribution models give all possible next states and rewards with probabilities, $p(s',r\mid s,a)$, as DP requires. Sample models produce one possible transition, sampled according to those probabilities (a simulator, game rules, a learned network); they are much easier to obtain.

Planning is any computation that takes a model and produces or improves a policy. State-space planning uses the same ingredients as learning: compute values by backups on (simulated) experience, then improve the policy. Q-learning applied to simulated transitions is random-sample one-step tabular Q-planning.

Model-free methods (MC, TD, policy gradients) learn directly from real experience. Model-based methods learn or are given a model and use it to plan; they are more sample-efficient but can suffer from model errors.

sections.title: Planning with Dyna-Q
sections.plain: Each real step teaches the value function and the model; then imagined steps from the model teach the value function more.
sections.body:
In Dyna, real experience is used in two ways: direct RL (update values/policy) and model learning (improve the model), and the model is then used for planning (simulated updates).

Tabular Dyna-Q
  1. S ← current state; A ← ε-greedy(S, Q).
  2. Take A; observe R, S′.
  3. Direct RL: Q(S, A) += α[R + γ maxₐ Q(S′, a) − Q(S, A)].
  4. Model learning: Model(S, A) ← R, S′ (deterministic environment assumed).
  5. Planning, repeat n times: S ← random previously observed state; A ← random action previously taken in S; R, S′ ← Model(S, A); Q-learning update on (S, A, R, S′).

Maze (ex1), 6×9 with walls, +1 at the goal, γ = 0.95 (averages over 10 runs): with n = 0 (plain Q-learning) episode 2 takes ~605 steps; with n = 5, ~168; with n = 50, ~45, and episodes 10–50 average 16.5 steps vs 41.5 without planning (shortest path 14). In the first episode only the transition into the goal gains value; planning propagates it backwards through the remembered transitions before the next real step.

sections.title: Dyna-Q+ and changing environments
sections.plain: When the world changes, a remembered model is wrong; reward the agent for re-checking stale transitions.
sections.body:
If the environment changes (a blocked path, a new shortcut), the model becomes incorrect. If it becomes pessimistic (a shortcut opens that the model doesn't know about), the planner never directs the agent to discover it. Dyna-Q+ keeps track of how long $\tau$ each state–action pair has gone untried and adds a bonus to simulated rewards:

$$r_{\text{plan}} = r + \kappa\sqrt{\tau}$$

This encourages behaviour that tests long-untried transitions, so changes are discovered. It is a form of exploration bonus (curiosity) that operates in planning, at the cost of some extra exploration in stationary environments.

sections.title: Upper confidence bounds for trees
sections.plain: Use the bandit UCB rule at every node of a search tree to decide which branch to explore.
sections.body:
Each node of a game tree is like a bandit over its children. UCB1 selects the child maximising

$$\text{UCB1} = \bar Q_{\text{child}} + c\sqrt{\frac{\ln N_{\text{parent}}}{n_{\text{child}}}}$$

with c ≈ √2. Applying it at every node is UCT (UCB applied to trees), the tree policy of MCTS.

Worked. Q = 0.6, c = 1.41, parent N = 100: a child visited n = 10 times scores $0.6 + 1.41\sqrt{\ln100/10} = 0.6 + 1.41\cdot0.679 = 1.557$; visited only n = 2 times: $0.6 + 1.41\sqrt{2.303} = 2.74$. The rarely visited child is explored next even with the same win rate.

sections.title: Monte Carlo tree search
sections.plain: Grow a search tree by repeatedly selecting, expanding, simulating and backing up.
sections.body:
MCTS is decision-time planning: at each move it builds a tree rooted at the current state, then acts and discards most of the tree. Each iteration has four steps:

  1. Selection: from the root, follow the tree policy (UCB1) to a node with unexpanded children.
  2. Expansion: add one or more children.
  3. Simulation: from a new node, play to the end with a fast rollout (default) policy.
  4. Backup: propagate the result up the path, updating visit counts and value estimates.

MCTS is an anytime algorithm (stop whenever time runs out; play the most-visited action), focuses effort on promising lines, and needs only a sample model (the game rules). In Nim (ex2) it finds the winning move from 10, 7 or 6 sticks within 50–2,000 simulations; from 21 sticks random rollouts make the three moves' win rates differ by only about 0.02, so it may still choose a weak move: rollout quality limits MCTS.

sections.title: From AlphaGo to MuZero
sections.plain: Learned networks guide and replace random rollouts; eventually even the rules are learned.
sections.body:
• AlphaGo: a supervised policy network trained on expert human moves, refined by RL through self-play; a value network predicting the winner; MCTS using the policy network as prior for selection and evaluating leaves by mixing the value network with fast rollouts.
  • AlphaGo Zero: no human data; one network with policy and value heads trained purely by self-play, where MCTS acts as a policy-improvement operator (the network is trained to match MCTS visit distributions and game outcomes); no rollouts.
  • AlphaZero: the same algorithm for chess, shogi and Go.
  • MuZero: not given the rules; learns a latent model predicting reward, value and policy, and plans with MCTS inside that learned latent space (Atari as well as board games).

The common theme: search (planning) improves the policy; learning distils the improved policy and better value estimates back into the network, which makes the next search better.

sections.title: Learned world models and model bias
sections.plain: Learn a predictive model of the world and train in imagination, but model errors compound.
sections.body:
World models learn compact latent dynamics from observations (images) and plan or train policies inside them: PlaNet plans in latent space; Dreamer learns actor and critic entirely from imagined latent rollouts, using far fewer real interactions.

Model bias. A model fitted to limited data is wrong somewhere, and a planner will find and exploit exactly those errors (imagined trajectories that look great but aren't real). Errors also compound over long imagined horizons: with 5% per-step error, a 20-step rollout can be off by more than 150% in the worst case. Remedies include short model rollouts mixed with real data (Dyna-style, MBPO), model ensembles to estimate uncertainty and avoid untrusted regions, latent-space models trained for prediction of value-relevant quantities, and continual model correction from fresh real experience.

sections.title: Further insights and misconceptions
sections.body:
• Prioritised sweeping focuses planning updates on state–action pairs whose values are likely to change most (large Bellman error), working backwards from changes, far more efficient than uniform Dyna planning.
  • Expected vs sample updates in planning trade accuracy per update against cost; with large branching factors sample updates usually win for a fixed compute budget.
  • Background vs decision-time planning: Dyna improves a global value function in the background; MCTS plans at decision time for the current state only.
  • Test-time search in LLMs (sampling and verifying multiple reasoning paths) echoes MCTS ideas.

code.title: Dyna-Q on a maze with 0, 5 and 50 planning steps
code.explain: Tabular Dyna-Q (direct RL, deterministic model learning, n random planning updates per real step), averaged over 10 seeds; prints episode lengths.
mistakes: Planning from state–action pairs never actually experienced.
Using the model in a stochastic environment as if it were deterministic.
code.notes: Planning makes the value of the goal flow backwards between real steps.
code.code:
"""Dyna-Q on a small maze: how planning steps from a learned model speed up learning.

6x9 maze with walls; start (2,0), goal (0,8); reward +1 on reaching the goal, else 0; gamma = 0.95.
Each real step: Q-learning update (direct RL), store (s,a) -> (r,s') in the model (model learning),
then n simulated updates from randomly chosen previously seen (s,a) (planning).
"""
import numpy as np
ROWS, COLS = 6, 9
WALLS = {(1, 2), (2, 2), (3, 2), (4, 5), (0, 7), (1, 7), (2, 7)}
START, GOAL = (2, 0), (0, 8)
MOVES = [(-1, 0), (0, 1), (1, 0), (0, -1)]
def step(s, a):
    r, c = s[0] + MOVES[a][0], s[1] + MOVES[a][1]
    if not (0 <= r < ROWS and 0 <= c < COLS) or (r, c) in WALLS: r, c = s
    return (r, c), (1.0 if (r, c) == GOAL else 0.0)

def dyna(n_plan, episodes=50, seed=0, alpha=0.1, eps=0.1, gamma=0.95):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed); Q = np.zeros((ROWS, COLS, 4)); model = {}; lengths = []
    for _ in range(episodes):
        s, n = START, 0
        while s != GOAL:
            a = int(rng.integers(4)) if rng.random() < eps else int(np.argmax(Q[s] + rng.random(4) * 1e-9))
            s2, r = step(s, a); n += 1
            Q[s][a] += alpha * (r + gamma * Q[s2].max() * (s2 != GOAL) - Q[s][a])    # direct RL
            model[(s, a)] = (r, s2)                                                   # model learning
            keys = list(model)
            for _ in range(n_plan):                                                   # planning
                ps, pa = keys[rng.integers(len(keys))]; pr, ps2 = model[(ps, pa)]
                Q[ps][pa] += alpha * (pr + gamma * Q[ps2].max() * (ps2 != GOAL) - Q[ps][pa])
            s = s2
        lengths.append(n)
    return np.array(lengths)
print(f"{'planning steps n':<18}{'episode 1':>10}{'episode 2':>10}{'episode 5':>10}{'eps 10-50 (mean)':>18}")
for n in (0, 5, 50):
    L = np.mean([dyna(n, seed=s) for s in range(10)], axis=0)
    print(f"{n:<18}{L[0]:10.0f}{L[1]:10.0f}{L[4]:10.0f}{L[9:].mean():18.1f}")
print("Shortest path is 14 steps; with epsilon = 0.1 exploration the average stays a little above that.")

code.title: UCB1 and MCTS (UCT) on Nim
code.explain: Reproduces the UCB1 values 1.557 and 2.74, then runs MCTS with random rollouts from several positions and reports visits and win rates per move.
mistakes: Backing up results from the wrong player's perspective.
Choosing the final move by win rate instead of visit count.
code.notes: From 21 sticks random rollouts barely separate the moves: a motivation for learned value networks.
code.code:
"""UCB1 numbers and Monte Carlo tree search (UCT) on a small game.

Game (Nim-21): 21 sticks, players alternately take 1-3; whoever takes the last stick wins.
Perfect play: leave a multiple of 4 to the opponent.
"""
import math, random
print("UCB1 = Q + c*sqrt(ln N / n):")
for n in (10, 2):
    print(f"  Q=0.6, c=1.41, N=100, n={n}: {0.6 + 1.41 * math.sqrt(math.log(100) / n):.3f}")

class Node:
    def __init__(self, sticks, parent=None, move=None):
        self.sticks, self.parent, self.move = sticks, parent, move
        self.children, self.N, self.W = [], 0, 0.0           # W: wins for the player who made `move`
        self.untried = [m for m in (1, 2, 3) if m <= sticks]
def rollout(sticks):
    turn = 0                                                   # 0 = player to move at this node
    while True:
        sticks -= random.choice([m for m in (1, 2, 3) if m <= sticks])
        if sticks == 0: return turn                            # player `turn` took the last stick
        turn ^= 1
def mcts(sticks, iters, c=1.41):
    root = Node(sticks)
    for _ in range(iters):
        node = root
        while not node.untried and node.children:              # 1. selection (UCB1 / UCT)
            node = max(node.children, key=lambda ch: ch.W / ch.N + c * math.sqrt(math.log(node.N) / ch.N))
        if node.untried:                                       # 2. expansion
            m = node.untried.pop(); child = Node(node.sticks - m, node, m); node.children.append(child); node = child
        if node.sticks == 0: winner_is_mover = True            # 3. simulation (random rollout)
        else: winner_is_mover = rollout(node.sticks) == 1      # rollout returns 0 if the next player wins
        while node:                                            # 4. backup, flipping perspective each ply
            node.N += 1; node.W += 1.0 if winner_is_mover else 0.0
            winner_is_mover = not winner_is_mover; node = node.parent
    best = max(root.children, key=lambda ch: ch.N)
    return best.move, {ch.move: (ch.N, round(ch.W / ch.N, 2)) for ch in root.children}
random.seed(0)
for sticks in (21, 10, 7, 6):
    for iters in (50, 2000):
        mv, stats = mcts(sticks, iters)
        print(f"sticks={sticks:>2}, {iters:>4} simulations: take {mv} -> leaves {sticks - mv:>2} "
              f"{'(multiple of 4: perfect)' if (sticks - mv) % 4 == 0 else ''}  visits/win-rate {stats}")
print("\nNear the end of the game MCTS finds the winning move quickly. From 21 sticks the win rates of the three")
print("moves differ by only ~0.02 under random rollouts, so even thousands of simulations may pick a weak move:")
print("noisy random rollouts are why AlphaGo-style systems replace them with learned value networks.")
